cases.abstract: Small demonstration sets leave visual imitation policies poorly supervised for the states they visit after execution errors. DMD augments wrist-camera demonstrations with synthesized nearby views and actions that guide the robot toward a later point on an expert trajectory. A pretrained conditional diffusion model is adapted using task demonstrations, exploratory play, or both; camera poses recovered from image sequences provide its view conditioning and the geometric action labels. Targeting a later frame avoids labels that reverse progress when a synthesized view has already passed the next demonstrated pose. Hardware evaluations cover pushing, stacking, pouring, and shirt hanging, plus cup arrangement with unseen objects in a new environment. In apple pushing, DMD achieves 100% success versus 30% for behavior cloning over ten trials per method. With eight task demonstrations and a view generator adapted only on play data, the corresponding rates are 80% and 20%. On five unseen cups in a new laboratory, augmenting Diffusion Policy raises success from 4/25 to 16/25, with both policies using rectified, center-cropped images. These gains support augmentation around recoverable deviations, not recovery after irreversible events such as spilling.
cases.methods: DMD turns view synthesis into policy supervision by pairing each generated image with a geometrically computed recovery action. Camera poses estimated from demonstration sequences supply training pairs consisting of a source image, a target image, and their relative transform. The generator is fine-tuned from a pretrained diffusion model while its latent-image codebook remains fixed. For augmentation, a small random camera displacement conditions synthesis of a view outside the recorded trajectory. The label is the relative transform from this virtual camera pose to a future expert pose, rather than simply the inverse perturbation. Choosing the third future frame reduces the risk that a generated view has already overshot the target and would receive an action pointing backward. Mixing these pairs with the original demonstrations supplies correction behavior without collecting expert responses at each perturbed state.
cases.results: Pouring illustrates why the augmented supervision matters beyond reducing image prediction error. With 49 demonstrations and 16 play trajectories used to adapt the view generator, DMD completes 80% of trials, whereas behavior cloning completes none in the same randomized pairwise evaluation. The baseline can rotate the source cup without moving it toward the receiving cup, allowing positional errors to grow during pouring. DMD's improvement is consistent with better correction of such deviations. A separate comparison using a generator adapted only on task demonstrations yields 70% success for DMD and 30% for behavior cloning, showing that play data are not required for an augmentation benefit. The two behavior-cloning rates come from different A/B tests, potentially under different lighting, so the 80% versus 70% DMD contrast does not by itself isolate the contribution of play data. Moreover, the method assumes perturbed states remain recoverable: returning toward an expert pose cannot undo beans already spilled.
cases.notes: Pushing success rates are ten-trial observations. The eight-demonstration setting uses play data to train the view generator, not only eight trajectories overall. Cup-arrangement comparisons use a retrained, rectified-image Diffusion Policy baseline, not the original fisheye configuration. Pouring comparisons are separate randomized A/B tests; their differing behavior-cloning rates prevent treating the DMD difference as a controlled play-data ablation.

cases.abstract: Fine bimanual manipulation demands both precise demonstration collection and policies that can sustain control over long, high-frequency trajectories. ALOHA provides an open-source teleoperation system built within a $20,000 budget, using joint-space control between paired leader and follower arms, customized parallel-jaw grippers, and four cameras. Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) learns sequences of joint-position targets from these demonstrations, reducing the effective decision horizon. Overlapping predictions are combined for the same execution timestep to retain visual feedback and smooth motion, while conditional variational training accommodates variation in human demonstrations. Evaluation spans two simulated tasks and six hardware tasks; most hardware policies use 50 demonstrations, with 100 for Thread Velcro. In 25-trial hardware evaluations, ACT achieves 88% success opening a sliding ziploc bag and 96% inserting a battery, whereas four comparison methods never progress beyond the first stage. A six-participant study also finds faster fine manipulation at 50Hz than at 5Hz. However, ACT completes only 20% of Thread Velcro trials, and preliminary candy-unwrapping evaluation yields no complete successes in ten trials. The combined system makes several fine manipulation behaviors accessible without eliminating perception difficulties or the hardware's limited force capacity.
cases.methods: ACT predicts a fixed-length chunk of future absolute joint targets from the current four camera images and follower joint positions. Demonstration labels use leader joint positions rather than follower motion, preserving commands whose tracking error determines applied force through the motor controllers. During training, a conditional variational encoder summarizes the demonstrated chunk and proprioception into a latent style variable to model human variability; the transformer policy reconstructs the sequence while regularization encourages a Gaussian prior. At deployment, the encoder is removed and the latent variable is fixed at zero. The policy is queried every timestep, and exponentially weighted predictions for that same timestep are averaged across overlapping chunks. This combines the shorter effective horizon of sequence prediction with continuous incorporation of observations, rather than executing an entire task open loop. Averaging predictions for one time index also avoids blending distinct neighboring actions that may need different targets.
cases.results: ACT's ablations distinguish gains from sequence prediction from gains tied to modeling human demonstrations. With temporal ensembling disabled, average success across two simulated tasks and both scripted and human datasets rises from 1% at a one-step chunk to 44% at 100 steps. Larger chunks slightly reduce success, consistent with a tradeoff between shortening the horizon and retaining reactive control. Adding chunking also improves BC-ConvMLP and VINN, so the benefit is not confined to ACT's transformer architecture. In a separate comparison aggregated over the two simulated tasks, removing conditional variational training lowers success with human data from 35.3% to 2%, while scarcely changing performance with scripted data. That contrast supports treating demonstration variability as a distinct learning problem. Temporal ensembling produces a smaller, method-dependent effect: after separate hyperparameter tuning, it adds 3.3 percentage points for ACT and four for BC-ConvMLP, but reduces VINN's performance. Thus neither longer chunks nor prediction averaging is uniformly beneficial in the tested settings.
cases.notes: Hardware policy comparisons use one training seed and 25 rollouts, whereas simulation uses three seeds with 50 evaluations each. Thread Velcro uses 100 demonstrations, not 50. Candy unwrapping's zero successes in ten initial trials differ from three of five candies opened under a later protocol allowing ten attempts per candy. The user study's 5Hz condition samples leader positions at 5Hz but sends interpolated targets at 50Hz. The implementation describes L1 reconstruction, although the training pseudocode lists MSE; the methods paragraph does not resolve this inconsistency.
